# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Older adults often make decisions while exerting physical effort, but it is unclear whether effort lowers the quality of the evidence they use, changes how much evidence they require, or neither. In total, `r v("n_final")` older adults judged whether two tones (auditory task) or two Gabor patches (visual task) were the same or different while holding a handgrip at 5% or 40% of their maximum force. Pupil size was recorded throughout. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model was fit to choices and response times. High effort shifted drift toward "same" on all trials (`r eff("crit")`). It did not credibly change the separation between drift on identical and different trials, the model's index of evidence quality (`r eff("qual")`). In observed accuracy, high effort lowered accuracy on the hardest discriminations by `r fmt_num(abs(v("acc_high_low_Hard", "pp")), 1)` percentage points (`r fmt_p(v("acc_high_low_Hard", "p"))`). Boundary separation increased by `r pct_s("bs")`, a change within the region of practical equivalence. The starting point did not change. High effort dilated the pupil during the grip. In `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` participants with usable pupil data, a larger task-evoked pupil response predicted wider boundaries on the same trial (`r pct_s("P3_bs")` per SD). That association tracked decision duration: pupil size just before the response did not predict boundary separation. Physical effort therefore changed how older adults mapped evidence onto responses, not the quality of that evidence.

# 1 Introduction {.unnumbered}

Many everyday decisions are made while the body is working: judging a gap in traffic while gripping a steering wheel, or reading a label while carrying groceries. Laboratory work shows that combining a cognitive task with a motor task costs older adults more than younger adults [@verhaeghen2003]. Sustained isometric force is one such motor demand. Effortful handgrip impairs cognitive control [@azer2021detrimental] and working memory [@azer2023] in older adults. Chapter 1 tested younger adults with the present grip manipulation. High effort lowered visual discrimination performance and increased pupil size in every task, but effort and task difficulty did not interact, suggesting that the two drew on separate resources at these effort levels. The present chapter asks how the same manipulation changes decision-making in older adults, using a model that separates the processes that accuracy and response time (RT) combine.

Accuracy and RT alone cannot say why performance changes under effort. Lower accuracy could mean that the stimulus was encoded less well, or that participants answered on less evidence. The drift-diffusion model separates these possibilities [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. It treats a two-choice decision as noisy evidence accumulating until it reaches one of two boundaries. The model has four parameters:

- **Drift rate (*v*):** the average direction and speed of accumulation.
- **Boundary separation (*a*):** how much evidence is required before responding.
- **Starting point (*z*):** a bias toward one response before the stimulus appears.
- **Non-decision time (*t*~0~):** encoding and response execution.

In older adults, the most consistent age differences are wider boundaries and longer non-decision times, whereas drift is often similar to that of younger adults on simple perceptual tasks [@ratcliff2001aging; @theisen2021age]. Older adults also set boundaries more conservatively than would maximize their reward rate [@starns2010effects]. The model therefore separates a loss of evidence quality from a change in caution. Both have been proposed as effects of physical effort.

The first account treats effort as a competitor for limited processing capacity [@kahneman1973attention; @wickens2008]. If holding a 40% grip uses capacity needed to compare the probe with the standard, evidence about the stimulus should become less informative. In a same–different task coded by response, this predicts a smaller difference between drift on trials with a different probe and drift on trials with an identical probe. Such a reduction in evidence quality differs from a uniform shift of drift toward one response on all trials. That second pattern is a change in the drift criterion: the reference against which evidence counts as favoring "same" or "different" [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. A uniform shift can lower accuracy on difficult different trials without any loss of evidence quality, so the two must be estimated separately.

The second account treats effort as a change in physiological state. Isometric handgrip engages the noradrenergic arousal system [@mather2020isometric]. Older adults also show larger physiological responses to cognitive demand than younger adults [@hess2012]. Arousal could change caution in either direction. If participants respond to the added demand by requiring more evidence, boundaries should widen under high effort. If they shorten trials to end the effort sooner, boundaries should narrow. The direction of the effort effect on boundary separation therefore distinguishes the two possibilities. A third possibility concerns the starting point: transient, pupil-linked arousal has been associated with smaller choice biases [@degee2020pupil], which predicts a starting point closer to neutral under high effort.

Pupil size provides a trial-by-trial index of this state. Pupil diameter tracks activity in the locus coeruleus and related brainstem nuclei [@joshi2016], and the task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) increases with processing demand [@beatty1982]. Physical and cognitive effort both affect pupil size [@azer2022joint]. In diffusion-model analyses, trial-wise pupil responses have been related to specific parameters. In a reinforcement-learning task, larger dilation on choices between similarly valued options predicted higher decision thresholds [@cavanagh2014]. Across several decision tasks, larger phasic responses predicted smaller choice biases [@degee2020pupil]. Pupil responses, however, also scale with decision uncertainty and response time [@urai2017]. A pupil–boundary association could therefore arise because longer decisions produce larger pupil responses, not because arousal set the boundary. Testing the direction of the relation requires pupil measures taken before the decision, as well as measures that end before the response.

We combined both approaches in older adults performing auditory and visual same–different tasks under low (5%) and high (40%) handgrip effort. The first analysis was a diffusion model of choices and RTs. It tested whether high effort reduced evidence quality (the capacity account), shifted the drift criterion, or changed boundary separation or starting point (the state accounts). The second analysis added trial-wise pupil measures to the same model. It tested which parameter tracked the TEPR, and whether pupil measures taken before the decision predicted boundary separation, as they would if arousal set caution.

# 2 Methods {.unnumbered}

## 2.1 Participants {.unnumbered}

Community-dwelling adults aged 60–90 years were recruited around the University of California, Riverside. All were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, and had no contraindication for MRI, no current psychotropic medication, no neurological disorder and no major systemic condition (including diabetes). Of `r v("n_enrolled")` enrolled participants, `r nw(v("n_excluded"))` were excluded (suspected mild cognitive impairment; possible essential tremor). That left `r v("n_final")` older adults (@tbl-demographics). Under the inclusion criteria, `r v("n_adt") + v("n_vdt") - v("n_final")` participants contributed data to both tasks and `r nw(2 * v("n_final") - v("n_adt") - v("n_vdt"))` to only one (auditory, `r v("n_adt")`; visual, `r v("n_vdt")`). Participants gave written informed consent and received course credit or payment. Procedures were approved by the University of California, Riverside Institutional Review Board.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Participant characteristics"
ch3_tbl_demographics(tbl$T1_demographics)
```

## 2.2 Task and stimuli {.unnumbered}

Participants performed an auditory discrimination task (ADT) and a visual discrimination task (VDT) in the MRI scanner while squeezing a dynamometer with the left hand (@fig-design). After a blank gray screen (1.5–4.5 s), a grip gauge appeared for 3 s with a target at 5% (low effort) or 40% (high effort) of the participant's maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). Participants held the grip until the probe ended. After a 0.25-s blank and a 0.5-s fixation dot, a standard and a probe stimulus (0.1 s each) were presented 0.5 s apart. In the ADT, the standard was a 1000-Hz tone, and the probe was identical or 8, 16, 32 or 64 Hz higher. In the VDT, the standard was a Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, 4°), and the probe was identical or had a contrast 0.06, 0.12, 0.24 or 0.48 higher. The two smaller offsets were grouped as Hard, the two larger as Easy, and identical probes as Standard.

In this response-signal procedure, participants withheld their response until a cue appeared 0.25 s after probe offset. They then had 3 s to answer "different" (right index finger) or "same" (right middle finger), followed by a confidence rating that is not analyzed here. Each task had five blocks of 30 trials. Each block crossed the five probe levels with the two effort levels, three times each, in pseudorandom order. Effort was therefore known before each trial, but the stimulus type was known only at probe onset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_design()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F1_design_model.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

## 2.3 Sessions and maximum voluntary contraction {.unnumbered}

The tasks were completed across three sessions on separate days. In Session 1, participants watched instructional videos and practiced at least 60 trials of each task without the grip, and their MVC was measured. They then practiced both tasks with the grip and confidence ratings until the experimenter judged that they understood them. In Sessions 2 and 3, participants performed one task each in the scanner (order counterbalanced), each preceded by a short practice block. MVC was the mean force across three maximal 5-s squeezes, with about 30 s of rest between them. It was measured again in the scanner in Session 2, and that value set the 5% and 40% targets in Sessions 2 and 3.

## 2.4 Apparatus {.unnumbered}

The task ran in Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997psychophysics; @kleiner2007s] in MATLAB R2022b. Visual stimuli were projected with a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies; 480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) and viewed through a head-coil mirror (effective viewing distance 12 cm). Sounds were delivered through MRI-compatible earbuds (Newmatic Medical; 30 dB noise reduction). Responses were recorded with a RESPONSEpixx button box, grip force with an MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs; 100 Hz) and pupil diameter with a TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies; 2000 Hz). The background was mid-gray. The gauge's force bar covered less than 1% of the screen, so it changed mean luminance by less than 1% between effort levels, in the direction that would constrict the pupil under high effort.

## 2.5 Behavioral data processing {.unnumbered}

RT was recorded from the response cue. For modeling it was measured from probe onset, by adding the fixed 0.35-s interval between probe onset and the cue, so that the decision clock starts when evidence becomes available and the non-decision time absorbs the enforced delay. Of `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_raw"))` recorded trials, `r nw(v("n_trials_negative_rt"))` with a negative RT were removed. A further `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_cutoff_excluded"))` with a cue-locked RT below 0.20 s were removed as anticipatory. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_primary"))` trials (Table S1). Cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s were used in sensitivity analyses. Overall accuracy was at or below .55 for `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants. They were retained in the primary analysis and excluded in a sensitivity analysis.

## 2.6 Pupillometry {.unnumbered}

Blinks and other artifacts were removed with the ET-remove-artifacts toolbox [@mather2020isometric] and checked visually. The signal was downsampled to 250 Hz and placed on a time axis starting at squeeze onset. We validated the axis against the light reflex that follows the display change at gauge offset: across `r v("dip_n_cells")` participant × task recordings, the median latency of that constriction was `r fmt_num(v("dip_latency_median"), 2)` s.

The task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) was the area under the curve from `r v("tepr_window_post_probe")` after probe onset (`r fmt_num(v("tepr_window_start"), 2)`–`r fmt_num(v("tepr_window_end"), 2)` s after squeeze onset). It was computed relative to the mean pupil size in the `r v("tepr_baseline_pre_probe")` before the probe (the interstimulus interval, `r fmt_num(v("tepr_baseline_start"), 2)`–`r fmt_num(v("tepr_baseline_end"), 2)` s). As in Chapter 1, this baseline separates the response to the probe from the slower dilation that builds up during the grip. The window starts 0.3 s after the probe to allow for pupil latency [@mathot2018] and covers the typical peak, 1–2 s after the stimulus [@dasilvacastanheira2021task]. Gaps longer than 250 ms were not bridged in the area computation. Because the window extends past the response on most trials, the TEPR includes post-decision processing; Section 2.8 describes how this was tested. Two further measures were the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before squeeze onset (pre-squeeze baseline) and the mean pupil size during the grip (`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_start"), 2)`–`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_end"), 2)` s), relative to the pre-squeeze baseline.

Trials entered the pupil analyses if at least 50% of samples were valid in both the pre-probe baseline and the TEPR window. Each participant × task cell needed at least 20 such trials. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_pupil_final_trials"))` trials from `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` participants (Figure S1), a subset of the behavioral sample selected on recording quality. Each pupil predictor was centered within participant × task × effort and divided by the participant's pooled within-cell SD. Its slope therefore reflects trial-to-trial fluctuation around the condition mean.

## 2.7 Drift-diffusion model {.unnumbered}

### 2.7.1 Response coding {.unnumbered}

Choices and probe-locked RTs were modeled with a Wiener diffusion model [@ratcliff2008diffusion], with "different" as the upper boundary and "same" as the lower boundary. Positive drift therefore moves toward "different". The starting point measures a bias toward one response. On Standard trials, drift is negative when evidence accumulates toward the correct "same" response.

### 2.7.2 Model specification {.unnumbered}

Models were fit jointly to both tasks in brms [@burkner2017brms] with CmdStan [@cmdstan2024], using an identity link for drift, log links for boundary separation (*a*) and non-decision time (*t*~0~), and a logit link for the starting point (*z*). The predictors in the primary model (M4) were:

- **Drift:** stimulus type (Standard, Hard, Easy), task, their interaction, effort and an effort × stimulus term.
- **Boundary separation:** stimulus type, task and effort.
- **Starting point:** task and effort.
- **Non-decision time:** an intercept only.

Participants had random intercepts on drift, boundary separation and starting point.

The effort main effect on drift shifts drift equally on all trials, toward "different" if positive and toward "same" if negative. This is a change in the drift criterion [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The effort × stimulus term (stimulus coded +1 for Hard and Easy, −1 for Standard) changes how far drift on different-stimulus trials lies from drift on Standard trials, which is a change in evidence quality.

The starting point did not depend on stimulus type, which could not be known before the trial. The boundary terms for stimulus type absorb RT differences between stimulus types. Because stimulus types were intermixed, those terms are not interpreted as strategic settings (Section 4.4). Non-decision time had no predictors because, in a response-signal design, it mainly absorbs the delay before the cue.

M4 was selected from a set of nested models that differed in how effort, stimulus type and task entered drift and boundary separation (Table S2; formulas in S6). Two variants of M4 were also fit: M4b added effort × task interactions on drift, and M4r added by-participant random effort slopes on drift and boundary separation.

### 2.7.3 Priors and estimation {.unnumbered}

Priors were weakly informative on the link scale (@supptbl-priors). The boundary-separation intercept was bounded between 0.3 and 5. Non-decision time was bounded between 0.02 s and 0.01 s below the shortest RT. Models used `r v("n_chains")` chains of `r fmt_int(v("n_iter"))` iterations, the first `r fmt_int(v("n_warmup"))` of them warmup (adapt_delta = `r fmt_num(v("adapt_delta"), 2)`, maximum tree depth `r v("max_treedepth")`). `r v("refit_models")` did not meet the convergence criterion at this length and were refit with `r fmt_int(v("n_iter_refit"))` iterations. A model was accepted if every parameter had R̂ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 400 and no divergent transitions [@vehtari2021rank]. Table S3 gives the diagnostics for every model.

## 2.8 Pupil-linked models {.unnumbered}

Each pupil-linked model added one pupil predictor to M4. Each was compared with an M4 baseline fit to the same trials. The TEPR was entered on the starting point (P1), on drift with a TEPR × stimulus term (P2) or on boundary separation (P3). The pre-squeeze baseline was entered on the starting point (P4) and on boundary separation (P5). Because the TEPR window overlapped the response, three further tests asked whether a TEPR–boundary association could reflect decision duration rather than pupil-linked state:

- P3 refit after removing the slowest 20% of trials in each participant × task cell (P3_rt);
- boundary separation predicted from the pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response (P7);
- boundary separation predicted from measures that precede the decision: the previous trial's TEPR within a block (P6) and the grip-period pupil size (P8).

Effort effects on pupil size were tested with paired *t* tests on participant means within each task. Only participants with valid trials at both effort levels were included.

## 2.9 Statistical inference {.unnumbered}

Effects are reported as posterior medians with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) and the posterior probability that the effect has the sign of its median. Whether an effect was negligible was judged against a region of practical equivalence [ROPE, @kruschke2018rejecting]:

- **Log boundary separation and logit starting point: ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_a"), 2)`.** This is about a 5% change in *a* and about 1 percentage point in *z* near its observed value.
- **Drift: ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_v"), 2)`.** This is about 1% of the drift difference between Standard and Easy trials.

The proportion of the posterior inside the ROPE is reported where it bears on whether an effect is negligible.

Models were compared with Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [PSIS-LOO, @vehtari2017practical]. Observations with Pareto *k* > 0.7 were handled with moment matching and exact refits. Afterwards, no observation in any compared model exceeded 0.7. Differences in expected log predictive density (ΔELPD) are reported with their SE, and differences smaller than about twice their SE were treated as uncertain.

Observed accuracy was analyzed with a binomial generalized linear mixed model (stimulus type × effort, plus task) in lme4 [@bates2015lme4]. Models with random effort slopes were singular, so the model used a random intercept for participant [@barr2013maximal; @bates2015parsimonious; @brauer2018lmm]. High − Low contrasts at each stimulus type were computed with emmeans [@lenth2024emmeans]. Model adequacy was checked with posterior predictive simulations of choice proportions and RT quantiles in each of the 12 task × stimulus × effort cells.

# 3 Results {.unnumbered}

## 3.1 Primary diffusion model {.unnumbered}

Allowing drift rate to differ between tasks improved out-of-sample prediction (M4 vs. M3: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", flip = TRUE)`). Allowing the effort effects to differ between tasks did not (M4b vs. M4: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4")`; @supptbl-model-comparison). M4 is therefore reported below.

**Stimulus and task effects.** The upper boundary corresponds to a "different" response. Drift was therefore negative on Standard trials, where "same" is correct, and positive on Easy trials (@fig-condition-params). Drift was also negative on Hard trials (low effort; ADT: `r cell_s("v_cell_ADT_Hard")`; VDT: `r cell_s("v_cell_VDT_Hard")`). These stimuli differed from the standard, but evidence still accumulated toward "same", so most Hard trials ended in an incorrect response. Relative to Standard trials, drift was higher on Hard (`r eff("diff_hard_v")`) and Easy trials (`r eff("diff_easy_v")`). Both differences were larger in the VDT than in the ADT (Hard × VDT: `r eff("task_hard_x_vdt")`; Easy × VDT: `r eff("task_easy_x_vdt")`). Boundary separation was narrower on Hard (`r eff("diff_hard_bs", pct = TRUE)`) and Easy trials (`r eff("diff_easy_bs", pct = TRUE)`) than on Standard trials. Standard, Hard and Easy trials were randomly intermixed, so these boundary differences cannot reflect a setting chosen before the trial [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. We treat them as descriptive (Section 4.4). Boundary separation did not differ between tasks (`r eff("task_bs", rope = TRUE)`). In both tasks the starting point lay closer to the "different" boundary (ADT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_ADT")`; VDT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_VDT")`), slightly less so in the VDT (`r eff("task_bias")`).


```{r}
#| label: fig-condition-params
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_condition_params()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F2_condition_parameters.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

**Effort effects.** Effort effects were estimated in the same model and are reported in the same way (@fig-effort-forest; @tbl-effort-effects). High effort shifted drift toward "same" on all trials (drift criterion: `r eff("crit")`). There was no evidence that it changed how strongly drift separated identical from different stimuli (evidence quality: `r eff("qual")`), although the interval does not rule out a small decline. Drift decreased on trials with a different comparison stimulus (`r eff("drift_diff_trials")`); on Standard trials the change was smaller and its interval included zero (`r eff("drift_same_trials")`). High effort widened the boundary by `r pct_s("bs")`. This change lay entirely within the region of practical equivalence (`r fmt_rope("bs")`). The starting point was unchanged (`r eff("bias", rope = TRUE)`).

In observed accuracy, high effort was associated with lower accuracy on Hard trials (High − Low: `r acc_s("acc_high_low_Hard")`). On Standard trials accuracy was slightly higher, a difference that was not significant (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Standard")`). Accuracy on Easy trials did not change (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Easy")`; @supptbl-acc-contrasts).

## 3.2 Robustness of the effort effects {.unnumbered}

The drift criterion shift was unchanged when the effort effects were allowed to vary across participants (M4r: `r eff("crit_M4r")`). The between-participant SD of that effect was small (`r est_s("sd_effort_M4r")`). The shift was also stable at RT cutoffs of 0.15 s (`r eff("crit_thr015")`) and 0.25 s (`r eff("crit_thr025")`). Excluding the `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants with near-chance accuracy left the point estimate unchanged. With N = `r v("n_subchance_remaining")`, however, the interval included zero (`r eff("crit_subchance")`). When effort effects were allowed to differ by task (M4b), the criterion shift was larger in the ADT (`r eff("crit_ADT_M4b")`) than in the VDT (`r eff("crit_VDT_M4b")`), but the task difference was uncertain (`r eff("m4b_effort_x_task")`). Evidence quality was null in every variant. The boundary effect was positive at the 0.25-s cutoff (`r eff("bs_thr025", pct = TRUE)`) and after the near-chance exclusion (`r eff("bs_subchance", pct = TRUE)`), but at the 0.15-s cutoff its interval included zero (`r eff("bs_thr015", pct = TRUE)`; @supptbl-robustness).

## 3.3 Pupil-linked decision dynamics {.unnumbered}

**Effort and pupil size.** High effort dilated the pupil during the grip period in both tasks (ADT: `r pt_s("grip_high_low_ADT")`; VDT: `r pt_s("grip_high_low_VDT")`). In the post-probe window, the direction of the effort effect depended on the baseline. Relative to the pre-probe baseline used for the TEPR, the response was smaller under high effort (ADT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_ADT_B1")`; VDT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_VDT_B1")`). Relative to the pre-squeeze baseline, it was larger in the ADT (`r pt_s("tepr_high_low_ADT_B0")`) and unchanged in the VDT (`r pt_s("tepr_high_low_VDT_B0")`; @supptbl-pupil-descriptives; @suppfig-tepr). In the pupil subsample, high effort widened the boundary (`r eff("P0_bs", pct = TRUE)`). The drift criterion shift had the same sign as in the full sample, with a wider interval (`r eff("P0_crit")`).

**Which parameter tracked the TEPR.** Trial-wise TEPR predicted boundary separation. Each within-person SD increase in TEPR widened the boundary by `r pct_s("P3_bs")` and improved out-of-sample prediction (P3: `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P3_vs_P0")`; @fig-pupil-boundary; @tbl-pupil-ordering). TEPR did not predict the starting point (P1: `r eff("P1_bias")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P1_vs_P0")`). In the drift model, higher TEPR was associated with weaker separation between identical and different stimuli (TEPR × stimulus: `r eff("P2_drift_tepr_x_stim")`), with a smaller and less certain predictive gain (`r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P2_vs_P0")`; @supptbl-pupil-models).

**Timing of the TEPR–boundary association.** The TEPR window overlapped the response on most trials, and TEPR correlated with RT within participants (`r fmt_r(v("tepr_rt_r", "r"), v("tepr_rt_r", "lo"), v("tepr_rt_r", "hi"))`). The association with boundary separation remained after the slowest 20% of trials in each participant and task were removed (P3_rt: `r pct_s("P3_rt_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P3rt_vs_P0rt")`). Pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response did not predict boundary separation (P7: `r pct_s("P7_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P7_vs_P0pre")`). Measures taken before the decision showed small associations in the same direction: previous-trial TEPR (P6: `r pct_s("P6_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P6_vs_P0lag")`) and pre-squeeze baseline pupil (P5: `r pct_s("P5_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P5_vs_P0base")`). Grip-period pupil showed a small association in the opposite direction (P8: `r pct_s("P8_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P8_vs_P0grip")`). Of the measures preceding the decision, only the previous-trial TEPR improved prediction by more than two standard errors.

## 3.4 Model adequacy {.unnumbered}

M4 reproduced the observed choice proportions in `r v("ppc_choice_inside_M4")` of 12 condition cells (@supptbl-ppc-choice). It fit the RT distributions less well. `r fmt_num(v("ppc_rt_inside_pct_M4"), 1)`% of observed RT quantiles fell inside the 95% predictive intervals, and observed median RTs were on average `r fmt_int(v("ppc_rt_median_bias_ms_M4"))` ms slower than predicted (@suppfig-ppc). The misfit was concentrated in minority responses ("different" on Standard trials, "same" on Easy trials and "different" on Hard trials), which were slower than predicted. Non-decision time tracked the RT cutoff: `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr015", "median"), 3)` s, `r fmt_num(v("t0_M4", "median"), 3)` s and `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr025", "median"), 3)` s at cutoffs of 0.15 s, 0.20 s and 0.25 s.

# 4 Discussion {.unnumbered}

We asked whether concurrent physical effort changes how older adults make perceptual decisions by reducing the quality of the evidence they accumulate, by changing how much evidence they require, or neither. High effort did not credibly reduce evidence quality. Instead it shifted drift toward "same" on all trials. That shift appeared as an accuracy cost on Hard trials and, if anything, a small gain on Standard trials. Effort widened boundary separation by about 2%, an amount inside the region of practical equivalence, and left the starting point unchanged. Within the pupil subsample, trials with a larger task-evoked pupil response had wider boundaries. The timing of that association, however, does not show that pupil-linked arousal preceded the adjustment.

## 4.1 Effort shifted the drift criterion, not evidence quality {.unnumbered}

A capacity account predicts that a concurrent grip draws on resources needed to evaluate the stimulus [@wickens2008]. That would reduce the separation between drift on identical and different trials. The effort × stimulus term, which measures that separation, was close to zero. Its interval allowed a small decline but not a large one. The effort effect was a shift common to all trials. In diffusion-model terms, this is a change in the drift criterion: the reference point against which evidence is evaluated as favoring one response or the other [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. Because the upper boundary was "different", the criterion shift lowers drift on trials with a different probe, so those trials more often end in "same". On Standard trials the same shift moves drift further toward the correct response. The accuracy pattern follows from this. The Hard-trial cost is the change that a capacity account would predict, but here it arises from a change in the criterion rather than a loss of evidence quality. Accuracy alone cannot separate the two, because Hard trials were the trials on which the shift was most consequential.

The pattern is consistent with Chapter 1. Difficulty and effort did not interact in younger adults, which suggested that the two draw on separate resources at these effort levels. In the present older sample, effort likewise did not reduce evidence quality. This chapter has no younger comparison group, though, so it cannot show that the criterion shift is specific to older adults. The two chapters also differ in tasks and analyses.

The boundary results do not support either account of how effort changes caution. An adaptive-caution account predicts wider boundaries under high effort; a fatigue account predicts narrower ones. The estimated change was positive but practically negligible, and its interval included zero at the shortest RT cutoff. The data therefore show no meaningful change in caution under a 40% MVC grip. The starting point was also unchanged, so effort did not alter the prior preference for either response.

## 4.2 Effort and pupil-linked arousal {.unnumbered}

High effort increased pupil size during the grip in both tasks, consistent with evidence that isometric handgrip engages the noradrenergic arousal system [@mather2020isometric]. The effect on the post-probe response depended on the baseline. Relative to the pupil size just before the probe, the response was smaller under high effort. Relative to the pupil size before the squeeze, it was larger in the auditory task. Together these indicate that high effort raised the pupil level that carried into the decision, and that the response to the probe added less on top of that level. Larger baseline pupil size has been associated with smaller task-evoked responses [@gilzenrat2010], in line with adaptive gain theory's distinction between tonic and phasic arousal [@astonjones2005]. Our design cannot separate a change in phasic responding from a ceiling on dilation. The smaller post-probe response therefore should not be read as lower arousal.

## 4.3 The TEPR–boundary association {.unnumbered}

Trial-wise TEPR predicted boundary separation better than any other pupil measure. This parallels work in which larger pupil dilation on high-conflict choices in a reinforcement-learning task predicted higher decision thresholds [@cavanagh2014]. Three results argue against reading the association as arousal causing caution:

- **Overlap with decision time.** The TEPR window overlapped the response, and TEPR correlated with RT within participants. A wider boundary lengthens the decision, and a longer decision lets more of the pupil response accumulate in the window. The association weakened when the slowest trials were removed, although it did not disappear.
- **No signal just before the response.** Pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response did not predict boundary separation.
- **Weak predictive gain from earlier measures.** Measures taken before the decision showed associations in the same direction. Only the previous-trial TEPR improved prediction reliably, and it may reflect the carry-over of slow decisions from one trial to the next rather than arousal.

The TEPR was also associated with weaker separation of identical and different stimuli in the drift model. This fits evidence that post-decision pupil responses scale with decision uncertainty [@urai2017]. Taken together, the TEPR tracked how long and how uncertain a decision was. Whether arousal before the decision sets the boundary remains open.

## 4.4 Limitations and future directions {.unnumbered}

**Boundary terms.** Boundary separation was allowed to vary with stimulus type, although stimulus types were intermixed and could not be anticipated. These terms let the model absorb RT differences between stimulus types that a diffusion model without across-trial variability cannot otherwise capture. This was most evident for minority responses, which were slower than predicted. That slow-error pattern is the signature of variability in drift across trials [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The effort contrasts were stable across model variants and RT cutoffs, but absolute parameter values depend on this choice. Models with across-trial variability in drift and non-decision time [@ratcliff2002estimating] would test whether the effort effects survive a better account of RT distributions.

**Response-signal design.** Because participants waited for a cue, non-decision time absorbed the enforced delay and changed almost one-for-one with the RT cutoff. It cannot be interpreted as encoding or motor time, and effort effects on it were not tested. The design also limits how much RT information constrains boundary separation. A free-response version of the task would test the boundary results more directly.

**Pupil sample and measure.** The pupil analyses used `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` of the `r v("n_final")` participants, selected on recording quality, and they are correlational at the level of trials. The effort effects in that subsample matched the full sample in direction. The TEPR window included post-decision processing, and the grip-period measure combined arousal with trial-to-trial variation in the force produced. Entering the recorded trial-wise grip force as a covariate would separate the two.

**Design.** With two effort levels, the study cannot test non-monotonic effects of arousal. Hard trials were answered incorrectly more often than correctly, so Hard-trial estimates reflect a strong bias toward "same" as well as low sensitivity. When participants with near-chance accuracy were excluded, the criterion shift kept its size, but its interval included zero. The effect is small and should be replicated.

## 4.5 Conclusion {.unnumbered}

In older adults, holding a 40% MVC grip during an auditory or visual same–different judgment shifted the drift criterion toward "same". It did not reduce the quality of the evidence accumulated or change response caution in a meaningful way. Larger task-evoked pupil responses accompanied wider decision boundaries from trial to trial, but this association mainly tracked decision duration and uncertainty. It does not show that arousal set the boundary.

## S12 Analysis provenance (dissertation only) {.unnumbered}

The pupil sample was built from a single generation of preprocessed pupil files. Each trial's time axis was reconstructed from the sample index and validated against the light reflex at gauge offset (Section 2.6). An earlier build mixed two file generations, one of which placed some trials on a stretched time axis. The rebuild corrected this and moved the quality criterion to the TEPR window itself. Relative to that earlier sample, `r fmt_int(v("n_pupil_entered_vs_r8"))` trials entered and `r fmt_int(v("n_pupil_left_vs_r8"))` left the pupil sample, and all conclusions were unchanged.

Of the 9,405 r8 trials with a finite TEPR, 1,599 were timed by placing samples evenly from −3.0 to 10.7 s, because stepping from −3.0 s by the file’s own interval did not end between 8 and 15 s. The r10 series keeps the 7,806 trials on the step clock, which drops every trial from BAP101, BAP124, BAP191, BAP194, BAP195, and BAP199 (594 trials) and 1,005 further trials from 12 participants who still contribute step-clock recordings.

:::


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (isTRUE(params$draft_watermark)) {
  if (isTRUE(knitr::is_latex_output())) {
    cat("\n\n```{=latex}\n\\FloatBarrier\n```\n\n")
  }
  cat("\n\n# Appendix: Response to advisor comments (draft only) {.unnumbered}\n\n")
  log_path <- file.path(proj_root, "reports", "ch3_comment_resolution_log.csv")
  comments <- utils::read.csv(log_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
  comments[is.na(comments)] <- ""
  comments$Section <- ifelse(nzchar(comments$new_section), comments$new_section, comments$july_section)
  if (isTRUE(knitr::is_latex_output())) {
    esc <- function(x) {
      x <- gsub("\\", "\\textbackslash{}", x, fixed = TRUE)
      x <- gsub("&", "\\&", x, fixed = TRUE)
      x <- gsub("%", "\\%", x, fixed = TRUE)
      x <- gsub("_", "\\_", x, fixed = TRUE)
      x <- gsub("#", "\\#", x, fixed = TRUE)
      x <- gsub("$", "\\$", x, fixed = TRUE)
    }
    cat("```{=latex}\n")
    cat("\\begingroup\n\\fontsize{8}{10}\\selectfont\n\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}\n")
    cat("\\begin{longtable}{@{}p{0.08\\linewidth}p{0.14\\linewidth}p{0.36\\linewidth}p{0.36\\linewidth}@{}}\n")
    cat("\\toprule\nID & Section & Comment & Response \\\\\n\\midrule\n\\endhead\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(comments))) {
      resp <- esc(comments$resolution[i])
      if (identical(comments$status[i], "open")) {
        resp <- paste0("\\textbf{Open} ", resp)
      }
      cat(sprintf(
        "%s & %s & %s & %s \\\\\n",
        esc(comments$comment_id[i]),
        esc(comments$Section[i]),
        esc(comments$comment_text[i]),
        resp
      ))
    }
    cat("\\bottomrule\n\\end{longtable}\n\\endgroup\n")
    cat("```\n")
  } else {
    pipe <- function(x) gsub("|", "/", x, fixed = TRUE)
    one <- function(x) pipe(gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", x))
    cat("| ID | Section | Comment | Response |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(comments))) {
      resp <- comments$resolution[i]
      if (identical(comments$status[i], "open")) {
        resp <- paste0("**Open** ", resp)
      }
      cat(sprintf(
        "| %s | %s | %s | %s |\n",
        one(comments$comment_id[i]),
        one(comments$Section[i]),
        one(comments$comment_text[i]),
        one(resp)
      ))
    }
    cat("\n")
  }
}
```
